meta.name: Scottish Terrier Puppy Checklist
meta.excerpt: A Scottish Terrier puppy arrives with strong opinions and a big personality in a small package. This checklist covers what to prepare, how to establish respectful mutual boundaries, and the training approach that works for this independent and dignified breed.
meta.meta_description: Scottish Terrier puppy checklist: supplies, secure yard setup, training approach, and socialization for the independent and iconic Scottie.

hero.alt: Eight-week-old Scottish Terrier puppy with soft black puppy coat

intro.label: Before Puppy Comes Home
intro.heading: What do you need before bringing home a Scottish Terrier puppy?
intro.html:
The Scottish Terrier puppy is compact, alert, and has a personality that becomes very apparent in the first days. Preparation focuses on secure containment, finding a breed-knowledgeable groomer, and knowing the vWD status of your puppy before any veterinary procedures.

This guide contains affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Wooffy earns from qualifying purchases.

Supplies Checklist

  • Medium wire crate with divider
  • Small, heavy stainless steel food and water bowls
  • Adjustable collar and 6-foot leash
  • Front-clip harness for leash training
  • ID tag with phone number
    One option: GoTags Personalized Stainless Steel ID Tag on Amazon. An engraved stainless steel ID tag; you pick the shape and the lines of text at checkout. Put a phone number that's actually answered on it, and update the engraving if you move.
  • Small-breed puppy food confirmed with breeder
    One option: Purina Pro Plan Small Breed Puppy, Chicken & Rice (6 lb) on Amazon. Purina Pro Plan's small-breed puppy formula, with kibble sized for small mouths and chicken as the first ingredient. Ask your vet about portions and when to move to adult food.
  • Slicker brush and wide-tooth metal comb
    One option: Chris Christensen Big G Slicker Brush on Amazon. Long angled pins in a flexible cushioned pad that lift dead hair and work through leg and beard furnishings. Use light strokes; slicker pins can scratch skin if pressed hard.
  • Soft pet wipes for daily beard care
  • Enzymatic cleaner for accidents
    One option: Rocco & Roxie Enzyme Stain & Odor Eliminator (32 oz) on Amazon. An enzyme stain and odor eliminator for urine, feces and vomit, carrying the Carpet and Rug Institute's seal for carpets. Spot-test on delicate fabrics first.
  • Durable chew toys — the Scottie is a committed chewer
    One option: Nylabone Puppy Pacifier Teething Chew on Amazon. A softer puppy-formula chew for teething mouths, labeled for puppies up to 25 pounds. Puppy-formula chews are for baby teeth; move to an adult chew once the adult teeth are in.

Yard and Home Safety

  • Inspect fencing and secure any gaps — the Scottie's digging instinct is genuine
  • Bury wire mesh along the fence line to prevent digging out
  • Remove unsupervised access to small animals (prey drive is present)
  • Secure electrical cords and small chewable hazards

Vet and Groomer Setup

  • Find a vet before the puppy arrives and inform them of the puppy's vWD status from the breeder's health documentation
  • Schedule first wellness exam within 48–72 hours
  • Ensure your vet notes the vWD status in the dog's permanent file
  • Enroll in pet insurance with cancer and hereditary condition coverage immediately
  • Find a groomer experienced with Scottish Terriers or similar wiry terrier breeds
  • Book a puppy introduction appointment at 10–12 weeks

care.label: First Week Setup
care.heading: What supplies does a Scottish Terrier puppy need?
care.html:
The Scottie puppy benefits from a calm, structured introduction. It is not typically as enthusiastically social as a Golden Retriever puppy — give it space to assess its new environment on its own terms.

Day 1–2

  • Show the puppy the crate with a meal inside — do not force; allow the puppy to investigate at its own pace
  • Begin house-training schedule immediately
  • Allow the puppy to explore a gated area of the home without overwhelming social pressure
  • Begin daily beard wiping as part of the post-meal routine from day one

Day 3–7

  • Begin short harness walks — loose-leash training from the first step
  • Introduce 1–2 calm adult visitors with quiet positive interactions — do not force the puppy to interact if it is hesitant
  • Begin daily handling: feet, beard, ears, and mouth for grooming tolerance
  • Complete vet wellness visit — remind vet of vWD status
  • Book puppy obedience class

Socialization (Weeks 8–16)

  • Calm adults — the Scottie is naturally reserved with strangers and benefits from positive, low-pressure introductions
  • Children who are calm and respectful — not boisterous young children
  • Other dogs in controlled, non-overwhelming settings
  • Novel environments, sounds, and surfaces
  • Building independence: crate time while home, increasing duration to prevent separation anxiety

special.label: Training
special.heading: Patient, Positive Training for an Independent Mind
special.html:
Training a Scottish Terrier requires a different mindset than training most breeds. The Scottie is not going to comply because you want it to — it evaluates whether the proposed transaction is worth its while. Your job is to make training worth the Scottie's while, consistently, and to never try to out-stubborn a Scottie (you won't win).

What Works

  • Very high-value food rewards — kibble is rarely motivating enough. Use small pieces of real meat, cheese, or other high-value treats.
    One option: Blue Buffalo Bits Soft Training Treats, Beef (19 oz) on Amazon. Soft, bite-size training treats with real beef as the first ingredient, small enough for rapid repetitions. Keep treats to about 10% of daily calories.
  • Short sessions (3–5 minutes) that end before the dog's interest flags
  • Consistent rules — the Scottie notices when rules change and will exploit inconsistency
  • A calm, matter-of-fact training style — the Scottie responds poorly to drama or pressure

Priority Commands

  • Come (recall) — this is the most important safety command and the most challenging for a terrier. Work on it daily in secure areas with extremely high-value rewards.
  • Sit, stay, down — the fundamentals. Work on them in short daily sessions.
  • Leave it — essential for managing prey drive around small animals and dropped food hazards
  • Off — teach this before jumping on people becomes a 22-pound habit

What to Avoid

  • Harsh corrections — the Scottie may respond with defensiveness, not compliance
  • Long repetitive drills — the Scottie gets bored and disengages
  • Expecting the same response every time in novel environments — work recall in many different places to build reliable response
  • Expecting the Scottie to be universally friendly — respect its selective nature rather than trying to force social behavior it's not comfortable with

Next up: your Scottish Terrier’s teenage months (roughly 6 months to 2 years)

  • How to teach a reliable recall — start before adolescence makes it harder
  • Leash reactivity — what to do if barking or lunging on leash starts

faq.q: Is the Scottish Terrier a difficult puppy to raise?
faq.a: It requires more patience and consistency than many small breeds. The Scottie's independence means it will test limits, may not respond as quickly to training as a biddable breed, and has a confidence that can be mistaken for stubbornness. Experienced dog owners find it rewarding; first-time owners sometimes find it challenging.

faq.q: What should I tell my vet about my Scottish Terrier's health?
faq.a: Ensure your vet knows your puppy's vWD (von Willebrand disease) status from the breeder's health testing documentation. vWD affects blood clotting, and knowing the status is important before any surgical procedure including spay or neuter. This information should be permanently noted in the dog's file.

faq.q: How do I introduce my Scottish Terrier puppy to strangers?
faq.a: Calmly and without pressure. Let the stranger crouch down to the dog's level rather than looming over it. Allow the puppy to approach in its own time. Use food rewards when the puppy chooses to interact. Never force a Scottie into an interaction it is resisting — this breeds defensiveness rather than acceptance.
